sentence: Male patient, 65 years old, smoker of 20-40 cigarettes/day and with a history of duodenal ulcer.

He had undergone surgery 5 years previously for stenosing neoplasia of the recto-sigmoid junction (Dukes stage B adenocarcinoma, T3N0M0, AJCC stage III-A), undergoing anterior resection, followed by end-to-end anastomosis by mechanical suture using the double stapling technique. .
The postoperative period of said intervention was uneventful and the patient was followed up every 6 months, with colonoscopy and ultrasound performed annually.
The endoscopic image of the perianastomotic region was normal in all revisions, including the last one, carried out the previous year (4 years after the intervention).

Five years after the intervention, the patient began to have soft stools, intermittent abdominal pain in the hypogastrium and later rectal bleeding, for which he was admitted to the internal medicine service, undergoing an abdominal CT scan, which revealed no pathological findings, and colonoscopy, in which a stenosis is observed 10 cm from the anal verge that prevents the passage of the endoscope.
A biopsy was performed in which no histopathological signs of malignant disease were observed and it was reported as a non-specific ulcer.
Given that the serum tumor markers were at normal levels, and in the absence of other signs of neoplasia, it was decided to repeat the endoscopy and perform an opaque enema.
The new endoscopy and biopsy showed identical findings to the previous ones.
In the opaque enema, an irregular colonic stenosis measuring 8 cm in length was observed, and the possibility of a malignant stenosis could not be ruled out with this image.

In the absence of conclusive evidence of tumor recurrence, a treatment period with corticosteroid enemas (budesonide, 2 mg in enema, twice a day) was decided, in order to reduce inflammation and thus be able to complete the endoscopic examination.

After a month, with the patient asymptomatic, the endoscopy was repeated, finding an inflammatory and ulcerated mucosa, covering a 6-8 cm long stenosis that can now be crossed with the endoscope, without signs of neoplasia being observed and the rest of the normal-looking colon.
The biopsies that were taken showed nonspecific inflammatory signs.
The stenosis is judged to be of ischemic origin and, given that the patient is completely asymptomatic, periodic follow-up is decided.
At 6 months of follow-up, electrocardiographic alterations were detected, for which a consultation with the cardiologist was requested.

Ergometry and coronary angiography revealed irregularities in the middle proximal anterior descending artery, severe involvement of the ostium of the diagonal branch, 80% stenosis of the obtuse marginal branch and 80% stenosis in the middle right coronary artery.
It was decided to dilate and implant a double coronary stent, after which the electrocardiographic alterations disappeared.
After 16 months of follow-up, the patient has normal transit and is asymptomatic.
